data_section_full_text:
4. Data

4.1 Samples

The data used in our analyses are collected from several sources. The conference calls are
obtained from StreetEvents, the product-similarity measure is obtained from the Hoberg-
Phillips data library, various financial data come from Compustat and CRSP, CEO com-
pensation and ownership data are from Equilar, and Chinese import data are from the UN
Comtrade database. Data availability from the intersection of these sources restricts our
sample to 14 years from 2003 to 2016. We retain firms incorporated in the US and listed
on the NYSE, Amex, or NASDAQ. We further exclude firms in the financial and utilities
sectors, which we define as the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) by MSCI
sectors 40 and 55.18 For firms included in the sample, we require all variables used in the
estimation to be non-missing and to have at least five responses in the Q&A portion of the
  17 To assess how well the organizations category as extracted by NER captures product names, we asked

skilled research assistants to identify the names of products in a random sample of 830 questions, each from
a different call. We then compared the Proprietary-information indicator implied by the NER organization
category with the indicator computed using manually identified product names. The out-of-sample accuracy
of the NER classifier of 78.67% suggests a non-trivial number of product names among organization names.
   18 We also exclude firms in finance (SIC codes 6000 to 6799) and utilities (SIC codes 4900 to 4949) according

to their SIC codes.

call.
   We consider two samples that differ in the unit of observation in each. The first
sample contains 2,703,717 question-answer pairs. The second sample contains 78,968 call-
level observations that correspond to 2,913 unique firms, with the number of firms in each
year ranging from 1,073 (2003) to 1,948 (2012). Table 1 provides the definitions of our
variables and descriptive statistics for our sample. The average total assets for firms in our
sample at $4.88 billion are about two times larger than the average assets of all firms in
Compustat over the same period at $2.52 billion.


4.2 Non-answers

In the question-answer-level data, the Non-answer measure corresponds to an indicator
variable that equals 1 if the response contains a non-answer phrase, and 0 otherwise. We
compute our Non-answer measure in the call-level sample as the non-answer rate for each
conference call, which is defined relative to the total number of responses at the Q&A
portion of the call. The average total number of responses per call is 34, with the 25th
percentile at 21 and the 75th percentile at 44 (untabulated).
   Figure 1 plots the average non-answer rate over time. The average non-answer rate is
stable at 11%, with the 25th percentile at around 5.7% and the 75th at around 15.4%. These
rates correspond to an average of 3.74 responses that contain non-answer phrases per call,
with the 25th percentile at 2 and the 75th percentile at 5. The average non-answer rates are
similar across industries. The lowest average rate is in the materials and energy sectors at
10%, and the highest is in telecommunication services and health care at 13%.
   In our main analyses, we use the all-encompassing Non-answer variable. This measure
includes refusal to provide an answer, Refuse, inability to provide an answer, Unable, and
a suggestion to discuss the question after the call, After-call.19 Table 1, Panel B, shows
Refuse is the most frequently used category, with a mean rate of 8.2% or 2.79 responses,
followed by Unable, with a mean rate of 3.7% or 1.26 responses. After-call is used less
often, with a mean rate of 0.2% or 0.07 responses. The rarity of After-call is not surprising
  19 Each response can include phrases falling into several categories of non-answers. For this reason, the

sum of the means of Refuse, Unable, and After-call exceeds the mean of Non-answer.

given that the Regulation Fair Disclosure was aimed at preventing management’s ability to
selectively convey material information, and thus would generally limit deferral to private
conversations after conference calls.


4.3 Performance

We use four measures of financial performance in our analyses. The first set captures
current performance and includes Loss and Return on assets. Loss is the indicator variable
for loss that equals 1 if return on assets is negative, and 0 otherwise. Return on assets is
defined as the ratio of earnings (IBQ) divided by lagged total assets (ATQ) measured for
the quarter of a call. The second set is intended to capture future performance. The two
measures we use are Return on assets, next, that is, Return on assets in the next quarter, and
Future profitability. Future profitability is the annual Return on assets averaged over fiscal years
t + 1, t + 2, and t + 3. We find 27% of the calls occur when the company has experienced a
loss, the mean (median) Return on assets is 0.3% (1.1%), Return on assets, next is 0.2% (1.1%),
and Future profitability is 0.9% (4.2%).


4.4 Competition

We measure competition using four different approaches. The first measure is the HHI,
which is the most common measure of competition in the disclosure research (Beyer et al.
2010; Cheynel and Ziv 2015). HHI is computed using quarterly sales for 3-digit SIC
industries, HHI SIC3. The mean (median) of HHI SIC3 is 0.156 (0.108), which is similar to
the mean (median) of HHI SIC3 at 0.143 (0.087) for Compustat firms over the same period.
   The second measure, Similarity, comes from text-based network industry classifications
(TNIC) developed in Hoberg and Phillips (2010) and Hoberg and Phillips (2016).20 This
measure is developed using product descriptions from firms’ annual 10-K reports. The
key assumption for this measures is that firms with similar product offerings use similar
words to describe their products, and thus, the textual similarity of product descriptions is
informative of the similarity of their product offerings. This measure is firm-specific and
  20 Hoberg and Phillips share their data at http://hobergphillips.usc.edu/

changes year by year as firms’ product descriptions change. Hoberg and Phillips (2016)
compute total similarity scores as the sum of the pairwise similarities between a firm and
all other firms in their sample for a given year. Thus, high total similarity scores are
indicative of a firm facing high levels of competition. Hoberg and Phillips (2016) show the
product-similarity measure explains discussions of high competition in the Management
Discussion and Analysis section of the 10-Ks, and that the similarity measure also identifies
firms’ self-reported peers from 10-Ks. For our sample, the mean (median) Similarity is 3.914
(1.853), which is lower than the mean (median) of Similarity at 9.39 (2.37) for all firms in
Hoberg and Phillips (2016) sample over the same period. Although lower, these differences
are not large given the standard deviation of Similarity at 16.1 in Hoberg and Phillips (2016)
sample.
   The third and fourth measures, Competition and SIC3-level comp., are competition mea-
sures similar to the ones developed by Li et al. (2013). These measures are based on counts
of the number of competition-related words, such as “competition” and “competitor,” ex-
cluding any cases where “not,” “less,” “few,” or “limited” precede the competition word
by three or fewer words. Li et al. (2013) count the number of these words in 10-K filings and
scale this number by the total number of words in 10-Ks. They argue this measure captures
management’s perception of the intensity of competition. We use a similar measurement
approach but focus on utterances by company representatives during both presentation
and Q&A sections of a conference call.21 For each transcript, we identify utterances that
contain competition-related words as defined in Li et al. (2013), and scale the number of
these utterances by the total number of utterances. We label this call-specific measure
Competition.
   We also compute an industry-specific measure for each 3-digit SIC code by taking the
average over call-specific measures for firms in each industry category, SIC3-level comp.
To compute the average for a specific call, we only include conference calls for other
firms in the same 3-digit SIC code that were held within three months before the call
being examined. Prior research suggests managers obfuscate poor performance (Li 2008)
  21 Utterances are defined as responses during the Q&A portion or spells of uninterrupted speech during

the presentation portion of the call.

and attribute poor performance to the effects of competition (Li et al. 2013). If attempts
to obfuscate poor performance extend to avoiding providing answers to questions, self-
reported competition and a higher rate of non-answers will be associated even absent a
causal relation. For this reason, when we compute SIC3-level comp., we exclude the firm’s
own call from this calculation. Although this variant of the measure is less subject to
issues of confounding, we expect it to be a less precise measure of the firm’s competitive
environment.
review_notes: The manuscript describes two principal observation units for the substantive performance and competition tests. The within-call and call-level samples overlap and their counts should not be added.
Table 2 is explicitly exploratory. The restricted Table 7 instrumental-variable subset is an additional test. Neither supplies a separate principal sample.
Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) and SIC are screen definitions. No separate acquisition route for those classifications is described.
